verdict.rationale: Both changes make the same correct fix: a Map from normalized email to the first index, with appended contacts added to the map so duplicates within the upload still merge and first-match semantics are kept. B also adds a performance test at the reported scale (30k into 50k), and the old O(n·m) implementation would fail it, so the speedup is protected. Its 2-second threshold is far above the expected tens of milliseconds, so flakiness risk is low. A's speedup claim rests only on a throwaway script, while B's report says plainly that it did not time the old version.
a_issues: No committed test guards against reintroducing the quadratic scan; the 79 ms figure comes from a throwaway script that cannot be reproduced.
b_issues: The wall-clock assertion in the unit suite could in principle be flaky on a heavily loaded CI machine.
The duplicate-existing test checks only phone fields, not ids, so it is slightly less explicit than A's version.

verdict.rationale: Both PRs make the same code change: a Map from normalized email to first index, updated on append. It keeps first-match semantics and merges duplicates within the upload. A adds a 30k-into-50k regression test with a generous 2s threshold, which guards against a return to the quadratic scan; B's tests cover only behavior, so a performance regression would go unnoticed. B's report is more informative because it cites a real ~79 ms measurement, but that does not outweigh the missing regression guard.
a_issues: The wall-clock assertion in a unit test can in principle flake on a very slow CI machine, though the margin is large.
The report never measured the speedup, and it asserts that any remaining slowness lies outside mergeContacts without having profiled anything.
b_issues: No committed test protects the performance improvement, which was the whole point of the task.
The 79 ms figure comes from an uncommitted throwaway script, so a reviewer cannot reproduce it.
